fields.title: Why Australia is the Best Country to Study Abroad in 2025
fields.content:
Every year, hundreds of thousands of students from Nepal, India, China, the Philippines, and dozens of other countries pack their bags and fly to Australia. And honestly? It's not hard to understand why.

Australia has quietly become one of the most sought-after study destinations in the world � not just because of its universities, but because of the entire experience it offers. From the quality of education to the lifestyle, the work opportunities, and the welcoming culture, studying in Australia is genuinely life-changing.

But what exactly makes Australia stand out from other popular destinations like the UK, USA, or Canada? Let's break it down honestly.

World-Class Universities That Are Recognised Everywhere

Australia is home to some of the finest universities in the world. The Group of Eight � which includes the University of Melbourne, Australian National University, University of Sydney, and five others � consistently ranks among the top 100 universities globally. These aren't just impressive numbers on paper. Employers across Asia, Europe, and North America actively seek graduates from Australian institutions.

What's more, Australian degrees follow a rigorous academic framework that is internationally recognised. Whether you're studying engineering, medicine, business, or the arts, your qualification carries real weight when you return home or apply for jobs anywhere in the world.

A Safe and Welcoming Country for International Students

Safety is one of the biggest concerns for students and their families when choosing a study destination. Australia ranks consistently among the safest countries in the world. Its cities � Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane, Adelaide, and Perth � regularly appear on lists of the world's most liveable cities.

Beyond physical safety, Australia has a strong culture of inclusion and multiculturalism. You will find communities from almost every country in the world in major Australian cities. There are Nepali restaurants in Melbourne, Indian grocery stores in Sydney, and cultural festivals celebrated across the country. You will never feel completely alone or out of place.

The Right to Work While You Study

One of the most practical advantages of studying in Australia is the ability to work part-time while completing your degree. Student visa holders can work up to 48 hours per fortnight during their studies and unlimited hours during semester breaks. This is a significant benefit that helps students cover living expenses and gain valuable local work experience at the same time.

Many students find part-time jobs in hospitality, retail, tutoring, and customer service. Some even find roles related to their field of study, which gives them a head start when they graduate.

Post-Study Work Opportunities

Australia has also made it easier for graduates to stay and work after completing their studies. Depending on where you studied and what you studied, you may be eligible for a Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) that allows you to live and work in Australia for two to six years after graduation. For students who studied in regional areas, this period can be even longer.

This post-study work pathway is one of the most generous among all major study destinations and is a huge draw for students who are thinking about long-term career prospects.

A Climate and Lifestyle Unlike Anywhere Else

Let's not forget the lifestyle. Australia's climate is warm and sunny for most of the year. The country has some of the most stunning natural landscapes on the planet � from the Great Barrier Reef and the Red Centre to rainforests and snow-capped mountains. Weekends can be spent at the beach, hiking in national parks, or exploring vibrant city food scenes.

Australian culture values balance. Work hard, but also enjoy your life. This philosophy filters into universities too � there is strong support for student wellbeing, mental health, and a healthy social life outside of academics.

Scholarships That Make It Affordable

The cost of studying in Australia can seem daunting at first. Tuition fees for international students typically range from AUD 20,000 to AUD 45,000 per year depending on the course and university. However, there are hundreds of scholarships available specifically for international students.

The Australian Government's Australia Awards Scholarships, the Destination Australia Scholarship, and university-specific scholarships can significantly reduce the financial burden. Many students from Nepal and other South Asian countries have fully funded their Australian education through these programmes.

Final Thoughts

Australia is not just a place to get a degree. It is a place where you grow, build connections, and prepare yourself for a genuinely global career. The combination of academic excellence, work rights, post-study pathways, safety, and lifestyle makes it a destination that is hard to beat.

If you are seriously considering studying abroad, Australia deserves to be at the top of your list.

fields.title: Complete Guide to Australian Student Visa (Subclass 500) in 2025
fields.content:
Getting your Australian student visa approved is one of the most important steps in your study abroad journey. It can also feel like one of the most stressful. But once you understand the process clearly, it becomes much more manageable.

This guide walks you through everything you need to know about the Australian Student Visa, officially known as Subclass 500.

What is the Subclass 500 Student Visa?

The Student visa (subclass 500) allows you to study full-time in Australia at a registered education provider. It covers everything from English language courses to undergraduate degrees, postgraduate programmes, and doctoral research. The visa is granted for the duration of your course plus a short period after completion.

Who Can Apply?

To be eligible for the student visa, you must:

- Have a Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) from a registered Australian education provider
- Meet English language requirements
- Have sufficient funds to cover tuition fees and living expenses
- Meet health and character requirements
- Have Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) for the duration of your stay

Documents You Will Need

Gathering the right documents is the foundation of a strong visa application. Here is what you will typically need:

Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE): This is issued by your university or college after you accept your offer and pay your initial tuition deposit.

Valid Passport: Your passport must be valid for at least six months beyond your intended period of stay in Australia.

Proof of Financial Capacity: You need to show that you can cover tuition fees, living costs (approximately AUD 21,041 per year as the current threshold), and return airfare. This can be shown through bank statements, scholarship letters, or a financial guarantee from a sponsor.

English Language Test Results: Most universities require IELTS, TOEFL, or PTE scores. Your visa application will ask for the same.

Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC): You must purchase OSHC before applying for the visa. Your university may arrange this for you, or you can purchase it independently from providers like Medibank, Bupa, or Allianz.

Genuine Temporary Entrant (GTE) Statement: This is a written statement explaining why you want to study in Australia and your intention to return home after your studies. This is one of the most important parts of your application and should be written carefully and honestly.

Academic Transcripts and Certificates: Copies of your previous academic qualifications.

How to Apply

All student visa applications are submitted online through the Australian Department of Home Affairs website (immi.homeaffairs.gov.au). There is no paper-based application process.

The application fee is currently AUD 710. This fee is non-refundable, so make sure your application is complete and accurate before submitting.

Processing Times

Processing times vary depending on your country of citizenship, the completeness of your application, and the time of year. Most applications are processed within four to six weeks, though some can take longer during peak periods (typically June to September when the academic year begins).

It is strongly recommended to apply at least three months before your intended travel date.

The Genuine Temporary Entrant Requirement

The GTE requirement is probably the single most important factor in student visa decisions. The Department of Home Affairs wants to be satisfied that you are coming to Australia primarily to study and that you intend to return to your home country after your studies.

When writing your GTE statement, be honest and specific. Explain your study plans, why you chose Australia and your specific university, how the qualification will help your career, and your ties to your home country (family, property, future job prospects).

A vague or generic GTE statement is one of the most common reasons for visa refusals.

Health Requirements

Most applicants will need to undergo a health examination with an approved panel physician before their visa is granted. The health check is arranged through the ImmiAccount portal and must be completed at an approved clinic.

After Your Visa is Granted

Once your visa is approved, you will receive a visa grant letter. Your visa conditions will be attached to your passport electronically � there is no physical visa sticker in most cases. Make sure you understand your visa conditions, including work rights and enrolment requirements, before you travel.

Final Advice

Start your visa application early, gather your documents carefully, and write your GTE statement honestly. If you are unsure about any part of the process, consider consulting a registered migration agent who can guide you through the application.

The student visa process is straightforward for most applicants who are genuinely intending to study. Prepare well, and you will be on your way to Australia before you know it.

fields.title: Cost of Living in Australia for International Students: A Realistic Breakdown
fields.content:
One of the first questions every student asks when considering Australia is: how much money will I actually need? Tuition fees are one part of the equation, but the cost of living is just as important � and often underestimated.

This guide gives you a realistic, honest breakdown of what it costs to live in Australia as an international student. Not the bare minimum survival budget, but a realistic picture of what most students actually spend.

Accommodation: Your Biggest Expense

Accommodation will likely be your largest monthly expense. Your options include on-campus student housing, shared apartments, homestays, and private rentals.

On-campus accommodation typically costs between AUD 250 and AUD 500 per week depending on the university and room type. It is convenient and social, but often fills up quickly so you need to apply early.

Shared apartments are the most popular choice among international students. Sharing a two or three-bedroom apartment with other students typically costs between AUD 150 and AUD 300 per week per person depending on the city. Sydney and Melbourne are the most expensive. Adelaide, Brisbane, and Perth are noticeably more affordable.

Homestays, where you live with an Australian family, cost roughly AUD 235 to AUD 325 per week and often include meals. This is a great option if you want to improve your English quickly and experience Australian family life.

City by City Comparison

Sydney is the most expensive city for accommodation. A room in a shared house in a suburb close to the city centre will typically cost AUD 200 to AUD 350 per week.

Melbourne is slightly more affordable than Sydney, with shared rooms ranging from AUD 180 to AUD 300 per week.

Brisbane, Adelaide, and Perth offer the best value. Shared accommodation in these cities can be found for AUD 130 to AUD 230 per week.

Food and Groceries

If you cook at home, you can manage your food budget quite well. Weekly groceries for one person typically cost between AUD 80 and AUD 120. Australian supermarkets like Coles, Woolworths, and Aldi are affordable and well-stocked.

Eating out is where costs add up quickly. A simple meal at a caf� or takeaway restaurant costs around AUD 15 to AUD 20. A sit-down restaurant meal is typically AUD 25 to AUD 40. If you eat out regularly, food costs can easily exceed AUD 400 per month.

Most students strike a balance � cooking most meals at home and treating themselves to eating out a few times per week.

Transport

Australia's major cities have reliable public transport systems including trains, buses, trams, and ferries. As a student, you are often eligible for a concession card that gives you discounted fares.

Monthly transport costs for a student who commutes to university by public transport are typically between AUD 80 and AUD 150 depending on the city and distance.

Owning a car is not necessary in most city areas, though it becomes more practical if you are studying in a regional location.

Phone and Internet

A SIM-only mobile plan with sufficient data for calls and internet usage costs around AUD 30 to AUD 50 per month. Providers like Optus, Telstra, Vodafone, and budget carriers like Aldi Mobile and Woolworths Mobile all offer competitive plans.

Home internet in a shared house typically adds AUD 20 to AUD 40 per person per month when split between housemates.

Entertainment and Social Activities

Australia has a lot to offer outside of the classroom. Movie tickets cost around AUD 20 to AUD 25. Gym memberships range from AUD 10 to AUD 60 per month depending on the facility. Many universities offer heavily subsidised gym access for students.

A realistic entertainment budget for most students is around AUD 100 to AUD 200 per month.

Monthly Budget Summary

Here is a realistic monthly estimate for an international student in Australia:

Accommodation: AUD 800 to AUD 1,400
Food and groceries: AUD 300 to AUD 500
Transport: AUD 80 to AUD 150
Phone and internet: AUD 50 to AUD 90
Entertainment: AUD 100 to AUD 200
Miscellaneous: AUD 100 to AUD 200

Total estimated monthly living cost: AUD 1,430 to AUD 2,540 per month, depending on the city and your lifestyle choices.

How to Reduce Your Living Costs

Cook at home as much as possible. Buy groceries from Aldi or look for discounts at Coles and Woolworths.
Live further from the city centre where rents are lower.
Use your student concession card for all public transport.
Take advantage of free activities � parks, beaches, library resources, and university events.
Work part-time. Many students cover a significant portion of their living costs through part-time work.

Final Thoughts

Living in Australia as an international student is absolutely manageable with proper planning. The key is to research costs before you arrive, set a realistic budget, and stick to it. Many students find that their part-time work income covers most or all of their living expenses once they are settled in.

Do not let the cost of living put you off. With the right approach, Australia is not just affordable � it is an experience worth every dollar.

fields.title: Group of Eight Universities in Australia: Are They Worth It?
fields.content:
If you have been researching Australian universities, you have probably come across the term "Group of Eight" or "Go8." It gets mentioned a lot � in university brochures, scholarship listings, and study abroad forums. But what does it actually mean, and does it make a real difference to your education and career?

What is the Group of Eight?

The Group of Eight is a coalition of Australia's eight leading research-intensive universities. These are:

- University of Melbourne
- Australian National University (ANU)
- University of Sydney
- University of Queensland
- University of Western Australia
- University of Adelaide
- Monash University
- UNSW Sydney

These universities share a commitment to research excellence, strong industry partnerships, and high academic standards. They collectively conduct the majority of Australia's university research and receive the largest share of competitive research funding.

How Did the Group of Eight Form?

The Go8 was formally established in 1999, though the member universities had been collaborating informally for years before that. The coalition was created to give these research-focused universities a unified voice in policy discussions with the Australian government.

Over time, the Go8 brand has become synonymous with prestige and quality in Australian higher education. Internationally, these universities are often compared to the Russell Group in the UK or the Ivy League in the US � though the comparison is not perfect.

Rankings and Global Recognition

All eight Go8 universities appear in the top 200 of the QS World University Rankings. The University of Melbourne and ANU consistently rank in the top 30 to 50 globally. UNSW, Monash, and the University of Sydney typically rank between 50 and 100.

These rankings carry real weight with international employers and academic institutions. If you are planning to pursue postgraduate studies abroad after completing your Australian degree, a Go8 qualification gives you a strong foundation.

Research Opportunities

One of the most significant advantages of studying at a Go8 university is access to world-class research facilities and opportunities. If you are interested in pursuing research � whether as an undergraduate research assistant or as a PhD student � the Go8 universities offer resources and supervision that are difficult to match elsewhere.

Many Go8 universities have strong partnerships with government agencies, hospitals, technology companies, and international research bodies. This means that research conducted at these institutions often has real-world impact and opens doors to careers in academia, government, and industry.

Graduate Employment Outcomes

Do employers prefer Go8 graduates? The honest answer is: it depends on the field and the employer.

In highly competitive fields like law, medicine, investment banking, and management consulting, the Go8 brand does carry weight. Graduate programmes at top firms often recruit heavily from Go8 campuses.

In many other fields � engineering, IT, education, nursing, social work � employers care more about your skills, experience, and attitude than the name of your university. A strong graduate from a non-Go8 university will often outcompete a disengaged graduate from a Go8 institution.

The bottom line is that a Go8 degree opens doors, but it does not guarantee success. What you do during your degree matters far more than the name on your certificate.

Are Go8 Universities More Expensive?

Generally, yes. Tuition fees at Go8 universities tend to be higher than at other Australian universities, particularly for international students. Fees for popular undergraduate programmes at Go8 universities typically range from AUD 35,000 to AUD 55,000 per year.

However, Go8 universities also offer some of the most generous scholarship programmes for international students. If you are a high-achieving student, the net cost after scholarships may be comparable to studying at a less prestigious institution.

Non-Go8 Universities: Underrated Options

It would be a mistake to dismiss non-Go8 universities. Institutions like the University of Technology Sydney, Deakin University, Curtin University, and Griffith University have outstanding programmes in specific fields and strong industry connections.

Many non-Go8 universities have invested heavily in practical, industry-focused education that produces highly employable graduates. In fields like nursing, design, information technology, and business, some non-Go8 universities consistently outperform their more prestigious counterparts in graduate employment rates.

So Should You Choose a Go8 University?

Choose a Go8 university if: you are interested in research, you are applying for fields where prestige matters, you have the academic profile to gain admission, and you can manage the higher fees.

Consider non-Go8 options if: you want a more affordable degree, you are studying in a field where practical skills matter more than prestige, or you want a smaller and more personalised learning environment.

The most important thing is to choose a university and programme that genuinely fits your goals � not just one with the most impressive name.

fields.title: Top Scholarships for Nepali Students to Study in Australia
fields.content:
Studying in Australia is a dream for many Nepali students. The world-class universities, post-study work opportunities, and the chance to experience life in one of the world's most liveable countries make it an incredibly appealing destination. But the cost can feel like an enormous barrier.

The good news is that there are real, accessible scholarships specifically designed to help Nepali students study in Australia. Some are fully funded. Others provide significant partial support. All of them are worth knowing about.

Australia Awards Scholarships

The Australia Awards Scholarship is the most prestigious and well-known scholarship available to students from Nepal. It is fully funded by the Australian Government and covers everything � tuition fees, return airfare, living allowance, health insurance, and academic support.

Australia Awards Scholarships are available for postgraduate study (Masters and PhD) at Australian universities. They are highly competitive, with selection based on academic merit and the potential to contribute to Nepal's development after returning home.

Applications open once a year, typically between February and April, and are submitted through the Australia Awards website. Nepali applicants must apply through the Australian Embassy in Kathmandu.

The key requirement is that scholarship recipients must return to Nepal for at least two years after completing their studies. This is a firm condition that cannot be waived.

Destination Australia Scholarships

The Destination Australia Programme is an Australian Government initiative that provides scholarships to international students who choose to study in regional Australia. Regional universities and study locations include towns and cities outside of Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth, and Adelaide.

Scholarships are worth up to AUD 15,000 per year and can be used for undergraduate, postgraduate, or vocational education programmes. Nepali students who are open to studying in regional areas have a strong chance of receiving this scholarship.

University-Specific Scholarships

Almost every Australian university offers merit-based scholarships for international students. These range from small tuition fee discounts to substantial awards covering a significant portion of fees.

Some of the most notable ones for Nepali students include:

University of Melbourne Graduate Research Scholarships: Covers full tuition and provides a living stipend for PhD students.

UNSW International Scholarships: Offers partial tuition fee reductions for high-achieving undergraduate and postgraduate applicants.

Monash International Merit Scholarship: Awards up to AUD 10,000 to exceptional international students.

University of Queensland International Scholarships: Multiple scholarship categories covering partial to full tuition for strong applicants.

ANU Chancellor's International Scholarship: Covers 100% of tuition fees for top-ranked international students applying to ANU.

Deakin Vice-Chancellor's International Scholarship: Provides a 25% to 50% reduction in tuition fees for eligible students.

Most university scholarships are awarded automatically based on your academic results when you apply for admission. You do not always need to submit a separate application � your strong academic record speaks for itself.

Aga Khan Foundation International Scholarship

The Aga Khan Foundation offers scholarships to outstanding students from developing countries, including Nepal, who have no other means of financing their studies. It covers postgraduate programmes only.

The scholarship provides up to 50% of funding as a grant and 50% as a loan. It is competitive and requires demonstrated financial need as well as academic excellence.

Nepal-Australia Community Scholarships

Several community organisations and diaspora groups run smaller scholarship and support funds for Nepali students in Australia. While these are typically smaller in value, they can provide meaningful financial support and also connect you with the Nepali community in your study city.

Tips for Winning Scholarships

Start early. Most major scholarship applications open six to twelve months before the academic year begins. Missing the deadline is the most common reason students miss out.

Focus on your GPA. Merit-based scholarships are won on academic performance. A strong academic record from your plus two or undergraduate study is your best asset.

Write a compelling personal statement. For scholarships like Australia Awards, your written application matters enormously. Be specific about your goals, your connection to Nepal's development, and how the scholarship will help you achieve them.

Apply to multiple scholarships. Do not put all your hopes on one application. Apply to the government scholarship and several university-specific awards simultaneously.

Final Thoughts

The financial barriers to studying in Australia are real, but they are not insurmountable. Thousands of Nepali students have funded their Australian education through scholarships, and there is no reason you cannot be one of them. Research your options carefully, prepare your applications thoroughly, and start the process early.

Australia is waiting.

fields.title: IELTS vs PTE vs TOEFL: Which English Test Should You Take for Australia?
fields.content:
If you are planning to study in Australia, one of the first practical decisions you will face is which English proficiency test to take. Most Australian universities accept IELTS, PTE Academic, and TOEFL iBT. But which one should you choose?

The answer depends on your strengths, your timeline, your budget, and the specific requirements of your university and visa application. This guide breaks down everything you need to know to make the right choice.

IELTS Academic

IELTS (International English Language Testing System) is the most widely recognised English test in Australia and around the world. It is accepted by every Australian university and by the Department of Home Affairs for student visa applications.

IELTS Academic tests four skills: Listening, Reading, Writing, and Speaking. The Speaking test is conducted face-to-face with a human examiner, which some students find more natural and less stressful than a computer-based format.

Scores are reported on a band scale from 0 to 9. Most Australian universities require an overall band of 6.5 with no individual band below 6.0 for undergraduate programmes, and 7.0 overall for most postgraduate programmes.

Test fee: Approximately NPR 28,000 to NPR 32,000 in Nepal.
Results: Available within 13 days of the test.
Test format: Paper-based or computer-delivered.
Valid for: 2 years.

PTE Academic

PTE Academic (Pearson Test of English Academic) is a fully computer-based test that has grown enormously in popularity among students applying to Australia. It is accepted by all Australian universities and by the Department of Home Affairs.

One of the biggest advantages of PTE Academic is the speed of results � scores are typically available within 48 hours of completing the test. This makes it ideal if you are working to a tight deadline.

The test is entirely computer-based, including the speaking component where you speak into a microphone rather than with a human examiner. Many students find this less intimidating. The test is also widely considered to be more predictable in its format, which means targeted preparation can be very effective.

Most Australian universities require a PTE overall score of 58 for undergraduate programmes and 64 for postgraduate programmes, though requirements vary by institution and course.

Test fee: Approximately NPR 25,000 to NPR 28,000 in Nepal.
Results: Within 48 hours.
Test format: Fully computer-based.
Valid for: 2 years.

TOEFL iBT

TOEFL iBT (Test of English as a Foreign Language, Internet-Based Test) is developed by ETS and is widely accepted internationally. However, it is slightly less commonly required in Australia compared to IELTS and PTE. While most Australian universities do accept TOEFL, it is worth checking individual university requirements before choosing this test.

TOEFL is entirely internet-based and tests Reading, Listening, Speaking, and Writing. Scores range from 0 to 120. Most Australian universities require a total score of around 79 to 94 for undergraduate programmes and higher for postgraduate study.

Test fee: Approximately USD 245 (around NPR 33,000).
Results: Within 4 to 8 days.
Test format: Fully internet-based.
Valid for: 2 years.

Which Test is Right for You?

Choose IELTS if: you are more comfortable speaking with a human examiner, you want the most universally recognised qualification, or your university has specific IELTS requirements.

Choose PTE if: you want fast results, you prefer a fully computer-based environment, you are applying close to a deadline, or you find the format more predictable with targeted preparation.

Choose TOEFL if: you are applying to universities that specifically list TOEFL as a preferred test, or you are also applying to universities outside Australia that prefer TOEFL.

Minimum Score Requirements at Popular Australian Universities

University of Melbourne: IELTS 6.5 (7.0 for many courses) / PTE 58 (65 for many courses)
University of Sydney: IELTS 6.5 overall / PTE 58 overall
UNSW Sydney: IELTS 6.5 overall / PTE 58 overall
Monash University: IELTS 6.5 overall / PTE 58 overall
University of Queensland: IELTS 6.5 overall / PTE 58 overall
ANU: IELTS 6.5 overall / PTE 58 overall

Tips for Preparing

Whichever test you choose, consistent daily practice is the most effective preparation strategy. Use official practice materials from the test provider. Focus extra attention on Writing and Speaking as these are the components where most students lose marks.

Consider taking a preparation course if self-study is not enough. Many language institutes in Kathmandu and Pokhara offer IELTS and PTE preparation courses.

Take a full practice test under timed conditions before your real exam to build confidence and identify weak areas.

Final Advice

There is no universally "easier" test � it depends on your personal strengths. Many students in Nepal find PTE slightly more predictable and appreciate the fast results. But if you are comfortable with face-to-face speaking, IELTS is equally achievable. The best test is the one you are best prepared for.

fields.title: How to Choose the Right University in Australia: 7 Things to Consider
fields.content:
With over 40 universities across Australia, choosing the right one can feel overwhelming. Rankings matter, but they are far from the only thing that should influence your decision. The right university for your friend may be completely wrong for you.

Here are seven things you should genuinely think about before making one of the biggest decisions of your life.

1. Course Quality in Your Specific Field

Overall university rankings are a useful starting point, but what matters most is how your specific course ranks. A university that sits outside the top 20 overall might have the best engineering or nursing programme in the country.

Research the specific school or faculty within the university that delivers your programme. Look at industry connections, research output in your field, and graduate employment outcomes for your course. These numbers tell a more useful story than overall rankings.

2. Location and Lifestyle

Where you live while studying will shape your entire experience. Sydney and Melbourne are vibrant, expensive, and packed with opportunities. Adelaide and Perth offer a more relaxed pace of life and lower cost of living. Brisbane has a growing tech and business scene with excellent weather. Regional areas offer unique lifestyle experiences and often come with financial incentives like regional scholarships and longer post-study work visas.

Think about what kind of environment you thrive in. Some students love the energy of a big city. Others prefer a quieter, more affordable setting where they can focus on their studies.

3. Tuition Fees and Available Scholarships

The difference in tuition fees between universities can be tens of thousands of dollars over the course of a degree. Before ruling out a more expensive university, research the scholarships it offers. Many prestigious universities offer merit scholarships that bring the net cost below that of a cheaper institution.

Conversely, do not assume a cheaper university is a poor choice. Many affordable universities deliver excellent education and strong employment outcomes.

4. Campus Facilities and Student Support

Visit the university's website and look carefully at what support services are available for international students. Good universities offer dedicated international student advisors, academic support programmes, English language assistance, mental health services, and career development resources.

These services make a real difference � especially in your first semester when everything is new and potentially overwhelming.

5. Industry Connections and Internship Opportunities

One of the most valuable things a university can offer is connections to industry. Universities with strong industry partnerships give you access to internships, work placements, guest lectures from industry professionals, and graduate recruitment events.

Ask each university: does the course include a work placement? What percentage of graduates find employment in their field within six months of graduating? These answers reveal a lot about the practical value of the education.

6. Student Community and Diversity

Check how many international students are enrolled at the university and where they come from. A diverse student community enriches your experience and helps you build a global network. Many universities have active student clubs and societies � cultural groups, professional associations, and social clubs � that make it easier to find your community.

7. Graduate Outcomes and Employment Rates

Ultimately, most students study in Australia to improve their career prospects. Look for publicly available data on graduate employment rates and median starting salaries for your field at each university you are considering.

The Quality Indicators for Learning and Teaching (QILT) website, run by the Australian Government, publishes detailed graduate outcomes data for every Australian university. This is one of the most useful research tools available and is completely free to use.

Making Your Final Decision

After researching all of these factors, shortlist two or three universities and courses. Reach out to each university's international admissions office with any specific questions. Many universities also have student ambassadors from Nepal or South Asia who can give you a genuine, honest perspective on student life.

Your university choice sets the stage for the next three or four years of your life. Take the time to get it right.

fields.title: Student Life in Melbourne: What to Expect as an International Student
fields.content:
Melbourne has a reputation. Ask any international student who has studied there and they will tell you the same thing: it gets under your skin. There is something about this city that makes people fall in love with it � and many students who came for two years end up staying for ten.

But what is student life in Melbourne actually like? Here is an honest picture based on the real experiences of international students.

A City Built for Students

Melbourne is home to several major universities including the University of Melbourne, Monash University, RMIT University, La Trobe University, Deakin University, and Swinburne University. Combined, these institutions attract hundreds of thousands of students from around the world. The city's entire infrastructure � its public transport, its cafes, its rental market, its nightlife � has evolved to accommodate this enormous student population.

You will not feel like an outsider in Melbourne. Walk through the CBD or Carlton or Fitzroy on any given day and you will hear dozens of languages. You will find restaurants representing every corner of the world. Melbourne's multicultural identity is not just a talking point � it is woven into the daily fabric of the city.

Accommodation in Melbourne

Most students arrive and spend their first few weeks figuring out accommodation. On-campus student housing at the University of Melbourne and RMIT fills up quickly, so if this is your preference, apply as early as possible � ideally before you even arrive in Australia.

The most popular option for most students is renting a room in a shared house. Suburbs like Carlton, Fitzroy, Footscray, Brunswick, and Coburg are popular among students for their proximity to universities and their affordable rents relative to the CBD.

Expect to pay between AUD 180 and AUD 320 per week for a room in a share house depending on the suburb and the quality of the property.

Food and the Melbourne Cafe Culture

Melbourne takes its food seriously. The city has a world-famous coffee culture � locals are genuinely passionate about their espresso � and an extraordinary range of restaurants, food markets, and street food vendors.

As an international student, you will have no trouble finding food from home. Melbourne has excellent Nepali, Indian, Chinese, Vietnamese, Ethiopian, Lebanese, and Italian options across the city. The Queen Victoria Market, the Prahran Market, and dozens of supermarkets offer affordable groceries for home cooking.

Getting Around

Melbourne's public transport network includes trains, trams, and buses. The tram network is the largest in the world and covers the inner city extensively. Many university campuses have tram stops directly outside.

You will need a Myki card for public transport. Student concession myki cards are available and offer significant discounts on fares. Monthly transport costs for most students range from AUD 80 to AUD 130.

Part-Time Work

The majority of international students in Melbourne work part-time to support their living costs. The city has a strong hospitality and retail sector that frequently employs international students. You will find opportunities in cafes, restaurants, supermarkets, and retail stores.

The minimum wage in Australia is one of the highest in the world, which means even part-time casual work pays reasonably well. Many students find that 15 to 20 hours of part-time work per week covers most of their living expenses.

Social Life and Things to Do

Melbourne has no shortage of things to do outside of study. The city has world-class museums and galleries � most of which are free. The Melbourne Museum, the National Gallery of Victoria, and the Immigration Museum are all worth visiting.

Sport is a religion in Melbourne. The city hosts major events including the Australian Open tennis, the Formula One Grand Prix, the Melbourne Cup horse race, and AFL (Australian Football League) matches that draw enormous crowds.

For students on a budget, Melbourne offers hundreds of free or low-cost activities: beach trips to St Kilda, hiking in the Dandenong Ranges, exploring street art in Fitzroy, or simply spending an afternoon in one of the city's many beautiful parks.

The Weather: Brace Yourself

Melburnians joke that their city has four seasons in one day. The weather is genuinely unpredictable � sunny mornings can turn into cold, rainy afternoons without warning. Always carry a light jacket, no matter what the forecast says.

Is Melbourne Right for You?

Melbourne suits students who enjoy a vibrant, multicultural, creative city environment. It is more expensive than Adelaide, Perth, or Brisbane, but the opportunities, the lifestyle, and the sheer energy of the place make it worth it for most students.

If you love food, culture, coffee, and city life � Melbourne will feel like home before you know it.

fields.title: What is a Temporary Graduate Visa (Subclass 485) and How Do You Get It?
fields.content:
One of the biggest advantages of studying in Australia compared to other countries is what happens after you graduate. Australia allows international graduates to stay and work in the country for two to six years after completing their degree through the Temporary Graduate visa, subclass 485.

This is not a small benefit. It is one of the most generous post-study work policies in the world and one of the main reasons Australia remains such an attractive destination for international students.

What is the Subclass 485 Visa?

The Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) allows international students who have recently graduated from an Australian educational institution to live, study, and work in Australia temporarily after their student visa expires.

There are two streams within the subclass 485 visa:

Graduate Work Stream: For graduates with qualifications in specific skilled occupations listed on Australia's skilled occupation lists. This visa is valid for 18 months.

Post-Study Work Stream: For graduates who have completed at least two years of study at a degree level or higher in Australia. This is the more popular stream and allows graduates to stay for two to six years depending on the qualification level and location of study.

How Long Can You Stay?

The length of the Post-Study Work Stream visa depends on your highest qualification:

Bachelor's degree: 2 years
Bachelor's (Honours), Masters by coursework, or Graduate Diploma: 3 years
Masters by Research: 4 years
Doctoral degree (PhD): 4 years

Importantly, if you studied in a regional area of Australia, you may be eligible for an additional year on top of these standard durations. This is part of Australia's effort to attract skilled graduates to regional communities.

Who is Eligible?

To be eligible for the subclass 485 Post-Study Work Stream, you must:

- Have held a student visa recently (within 6 months of applying)
- Have studied in Australia for at least 16 calendar months
- Have completed at least one degree, diploma, or trade qualification in Australia
- Meet health and character requirements
- Have health insurance

Work Rights on the 485 Visa

One of the most attractive features of the 485 visa is that it comes with full work rights. There is no limit on the hours you can work per week while holding this visa. This gives you the freedom to gain valuable Australian work experience in your field, build your professional network, and potentially transition to a longer-term skilled worker visa.

Many graduates use their 485 visa period to find a full-time job in their field and then apply for permanent residency through the Skilled Independent visa (subclass 189) or Employer Sponsored visas.

How to Apply

Applications for the subclass 485 visa are submitted online through the Australian Department of Home Affairs website. You should apply before your student visa expires � ideally within a few months of completing your studies.

The application fee is currently AUD 1,905. Processing times vary but are generally between four to eight months. You can continue living and working in Australia while your application is being processed if you apply before your current visa expires.

Documents you will need include:

- Proof of completed Australian qualifications (transcripts and degree certificate)
- Skills assessment (for Graduate Work Stream only)
- Proof of health insurance
- Health examination results
- Character documents (police clearance from countries where you have lived for 12 months or more)

Planning Ahead

If you are planning to apply for the 485 visa, it is worth thinking about this before you even finish your studies. Make sure your qualification meets the eligibility requirements, keep records of all your academic documents, and be aware of the six-month application window after your student visa expires.

The 485 visa is not a pathway to permanent residency on its own � it is a temporary visa that gives you time to gain experience and explore permanent residency options. Use the time wisely: work in your field, build your skills, get licensed or registered if your profession requires it, and start exploring what permanent residency pathways might suit you.

The Bigger Picture

For many international students, the 485 visa is the beginning of a longer journey in Australia. The post-study work period gives you real professional experience in a developed economy, which is valuable whether you ultimately settle in Australia or return home with internationally recognised skills and credentials.

It is one of the most valuable benefits of studying in Australia � and it is worth understanding thoroughly before you choose where to study.

fields.title: 10 Mistakes International Students Make Before Coming to Australia
fields.content:
Every year, thousands of international students arrive in Australia underprepared. Not because they are not smart or capable � but because nobody told them what to expect. Here are ten common mistakes students make before and during their arrival in Australia, and how to avoid them.

1. Applying Too Late

Australian universities have multiple intake periods � typically February and July � but scholarship and admission deadlines can be six to twelve months before the start date. Many students start researching too late and miss the best opportunities.

Start your research at least 12 months before your intended start date. Apply for scholarships as soon as applications open. Give yourself time to gather documents, sit your English test, and process your visa without rushing.

2. Choosing a University Based on Rankings Alone

Overall university rankings are useful but incomplete. A university ranked 200th globally might have the best programme in your specific field. Focus on course quality, graduate employment rates, industry connections, and available scholarships � not just the prestige of the institution.

3. Underestimating Living Costs

Many students arrive in Australia with a budget based on tuition fees and a rough estimate of living expenses. They do not account for bond and advance rent on arrival, buying household items for a new place, transport costs in the first few weeks before settling, or unexpected expenses like medical costs and replacing items left at home.

Bring more money than you think you will need for the first two months. The initial setup costs are always higher than expected.

4. Not Reading Their Visa Conditions

Student visa conditions include rules about enrolment (you must remain enrolled full-time), work rights (hours limits apply during semester), and attendance requirements. Violating these conditions can put your visa at risk.

Read your visa grant letter carefully. Understand every condition before you travel.

5. Ignoring the Genuine Temporary Entrant Statement

The GTE statement for your student visa is not a formality � it is a genuine assessment of your intentions. Students who write vague, generic, or dishonest GTE statements risk visa refusal. Be specific, honest, and thoughtful.

6. Not Arranging Accommodation Before Arriving

Some students arrive in Australia without confirmed accommodation, planning to "sort it out when they get there." This is stressful and expensive. Short-term accommodation in Australian cities is very costly. Rental markets in Sydney and Melbourne are competitive and move quickly.

Research and secure accommodation before you arrive. Even if it is temporary student housing for the first semester, having a confirmed address makes everything easier � including opening a bank account and getting a SIM card.

7. Choosing the Wrong English Test

Not all universities accept all English tests equally. Some have specific minimum scores for IELTS that differ from PTE equivalents. Check the exact requirements of your course before sitting your test, and make sure your score meets the specific component requirements � not just the overall score.

8. Not Researching Part-Time Work Before Arriving

Having a part-time job lined up, or at least a clear plan for finding one, makes a huge difference to your financial situation in the early months. Research the local job market in your city, update your resume to Australian standards (one to two pages, no photo, Australian phone number and address), and start applying early.

9. Failing to Connect with the Student Community

Some students arrive, attend classes, go home, and repeat � without ever connecting with other students or the broader community. This leads to isolation and makes the experience far harder than it needs to be.

Join clubs and societies at your university. Attend orientation events. Say yes to social invitations even when you are tired. The friendships you build in your first few months in Australia will carry you through the hard times.

10. Not Taking Mental Health Seriously

Moving to a new country is exciting but also genuinely difficult. Homesickness, academic pressure, financial stress, and cultural adjustment can take a serious toll. Many students feel embarrassed to admit they are struggling.

Australian universities take student mental health very seriously. Every university has free counselling services available to international students. Use them if you need them � there is no shame in asking for support.

Final Thought

Australia will challenge you, surprise you, and ultimately reward you if you approach it with preparation and openness. Avoid these mistakes, plan carefully, and give yourself permission to ask for help when you need it. Your Australian experience will be all the better for it.
